title: MLB Power Rankings: It’s time to check in on the new guys
author: Tim Britton
content:
Every week,​ we​ ask a selected group of our baseball​ writers​ — local and national — to rank the teams from first to worst. Here are the collective results.

Baseball executives will tell you that their first legitimate check-in on their team comes closer to Memorial Day or at least 40 games in. By that point, your performance has less to do with some scheduling abnormalities — how many times are the Rockies and Astros going to play this season? — and injuries and aberrational slumps than with true talent.

Fan bases? They don’t wait that long, especially when it comes to players they don’t know. Back when I, Tim Britton, covered the Red Sox, Mookie Betts went 1-for-10 in his first three big-league games. “This guy sucks,” someone tweeted at me. “Who’s next?”

So we split the difference and waited at least 20 games to gauge how the sport’s newcomers — offseason acquisitions with a new club or prospects reaching the majors for the first time — are performing in 2026. As for that fan who dismissed Betts? I hope they’re really keen on Connor Wong’s strong start this season.

All stats are through Monday morning unless noted.

Record: 16-6
Last Power Ranking: 1

Best newcomer: Kyle Tucker

Tucker has settled in nicely after a rocky first week, slashing .288/.386/.458 (.843 OPS) since April 3. He’ll be fine, and the Dodgers clearly are deep enough to weather slow starts. But are alarm bells sounding about their new closer, Edwin Díaz? After surrendering three runs to the Rangers on April 10, Díaz didn’t pitch for nine days, only to return Sunday in Colorado and give up another three runs without recording an out. Is he OK? (Editor’s note: Diaz was placed on the IL Monday due to what the team called “loose bodies” in his elbow.)

But let’s end with another new guy, rookie Ryan Ward, called up for the first time after 696 minor-league games. He singled twice in his debut. — Stephen J. Nesbitt

Record: 16-7
Last Power Ranking: 3

Best newcomer: Dominic Smith

Robert Suárez has been pivotal to Atlanta’s late-game lockdown pen, and Mauricio Dubon has more than held the fort down for Ha-Seong Kim at shortstop. But let’s spend a few words celebrating Smith, one of the dozens of players who submitted career years in 2020 but struggled to validate them afterward. On his sixth team in the last five years, Smith hit a walk-off grand slam in his first game with Atlanta and hasn’t slowed down since. A team that figured to have a DH surplus lost it when Sean Murphy went down and Jurickson Profar was suspended. Smith has capitalized. — Tim Britton

Record: 13-9
Last Power Ranking: 2

Best newcomer: Ryan Weathers

We’re used to limited choices for this category when it’s the Rays or Marlins or the like, but it’s odd how little the Yankees have received from newcomers. Offensively, Randal Grichuk is the only player to step into the box who wasn’t a Yankee last year; he’s 2-for-20. On the mound, Weathers’ four starts and Angel Chivilli’s two outs are the only ones from newcomers. The good news is that Weathers would win this for a lot of teams, especially after another gem Sunday. His strikeout rate is up above 30 percent, and this is about as good as he’s looked when healthy (knock on wood) in his career. — Britton

Record: 13-9
Last Power Ranking: T-8

Best newcomer: Edward Cabrera

After watching him with a keen eye over the last two seasons, Jed Hoyer’s front office finally executed a trade to bring the right-hander from Miami to the Windy City. Consider the move a win, as Cabrera has pitched 22 2/3 innings of 2.38 ERA ball. He’s gone six innings in two of his four starts and at least five in the other pair. His addition is particularly serendipitous as Cade Horton is out for the season, Justin Steele is still working his way back from surgery and Matthew Boyd is on the 15-day IL. Elsewhere, three relievers, including closer Daniel Palencia, are on the IL. That Cabrera is healthy, has been effective and is able to post has been a major benefit for the Cubs in the early going. — Johnny Flores Jr.

Record: 15-7
Last Power Ranking: 7

Best newcomer: Bradgley Rodriguez

The Padres’ 2.91 bullpen ERA has a lot to do with Mason Miller and his scoreless season so far, but tip your cap to the basically-new-guy Rodriguez, who, in 20 innings between this season and a cup of coffee last year, has a 0.90 ERA. Rodriguez could be pitching his way into a more important role for the Friars.

Among the other newcomers for the surging San Diegans: Walker Buehler and Germán Márquez have been steady through four starts apiece, Miguel Andujar has come out swinging — surprisingly, far better against righties than lefties so far — and Ty France has been slightly below average. The clock is ticking on Nick Castellanos and his .450 OPS. — Nesbitt

Record: 12-11
Last Power Ranking: T-8

Best newcomer: Framber Valdez

Save for an eight-run blow-up against the Twins on April 8, Valdez has largely been as advertised for the Tigers. He opened the season with 12 innings of one-run ball, then in his first start since that blow-up, he tossed seven innings in a no-decision. The groundballs are flowing, and the innings are piling up. That is precisely what Detroit signed up for when it inked the southpaw to a three-year, $115 million contract. Of note: he’s yet to allow a home run this season. Having half of your starts take place at Comerica Park helps, but Valdez has always been a maestro in limiting hard contact. — Flores

Record: 13-9
Last Power Ranking: 11

Best newcomer: Take your pick

So far this season, the Pirates are learning that good things usually happen when you spend money in the offseason or make trades. So as far as the best newcomer is concerned, well, take your pick. Among qualified second basemen, Brandon Lowe leads in homers and slugging and is second in OPS. Ryan O’Hearn is in the top 5 of first basemen by wRC+ (162). Gregory Soto has a 0.77 ERA through 11 2/3 innings, and even Marcell Ozuna, who weathered some early criticism, is slugging .633 over his last seven games. Together, they’ve helped Pittsburgh remain above .500 and in contention in a wide-open NL Central. — Flores

Record: 12-9
Last Power Ranking: 5

Best newcomer: Gary Sánchez

No longer seen as a franchise-altering backstop, the former AL Rookie of the Year runner-up has since morphed into a mercenary journeyman, bouncing from team to team in need of a serviceable back-up catcher with a potent bat. This year, Milwaukee has employed Sánchez’s services for the second time in three seasons. So far, the Brewers’ $1.75 million risk has paid off. Sanchez has a .238/.429/.619 slash line, his contributions are worth 0.5 fWAR so far, more than he put up in 2024 or 2025. The latest wrinkle? A walk rate in the 100th percentile (25.5 percent), the highest ever in his 12-year career. — Flores

Record: 11-11
Last Power Ranking: 12

Best newcomer: Brandon Nimmo

Take a bow, Chris Young. Nimmo has been a top-20 hitter so far this season, slashing .311/.386/.522 (.908 OPS) and leading the league in hits. While citing small-sample WAR totals is irresponsible behavior, let’s do it anyway, for fun: Nimmo has been worth 1 WAR. Marcus Semien? 0.1 fWAR.

Meanwhile, MacKenzie Gore has been mostly good early through five starts in Texas, and the Rangers bullpen, ranked third in baseball in ERA (2.91), has been propelled by savvy bargain adds: Jakob Junis, Tyler Alexander and Jalen Beeks. It hasn’t all been gold — Andrew McCutchen has cooled off after a hot start, and Danny Jansen started slow — but so far, so good in Arlington. — Nesbitt

Record: 13-9
Last Power Ranking: 22

Best newcomer: Michael Soroka

Much of the Diamondbacks’ winter was spent bringing back familiar faces who can’t possibly be described as newcomers, like Zac Gallen, Merrill Kelly and Paul Sewald. (Early returns there? Good!) But Soroka is truly new, and he’s made a heck of an impression. He’s 4-0 with a 2.78 ERA through four starts, racking up high strikeout totals few expected. On the flip side, Nolan Arenado (.556 OPS) and Carlos Santana (2-for-24 before an adductor strain) have made poorer first impressions. In Sanata’s absence, rookie José Fernández has seized the opportunity, hitting .300 so far while bouncing all around the infield. — Nesbitt

Record: 10-14
Last Power Ranking: 4

Best newcomer: Brendan Donovan

If we accept that Josh Naylor is no longer a new guy in Seattle, Donovan stands as the Mariners’ most vital offseason addition. Donovan may need time to adjust to third base, a position he rarely played in St. Louis, but he has more than delivered at the plate, leading off and batting .304 with a .954 OPS through his first 18 games in Seattle. The Mariners have needed that stability, as Cal Raleigh, Julio Rodríguez and Naylor have stumbled out of the gate. Newcomer bench bats Rob Refsnyder and Connor Joe have yet to find their footing, but there’s better news in the bullpen: lefty Jose A. Ferrer, acquired in the Harry Ford trade, has begun earning leverage opportunities. That Mariners ‘pen has some arms. — Nesbitt

Record: 13-11
Last Power Ranking: 17

Best newcomer: Does Chase DeLauter count?

The Guardians shockingly didn’t spend much this offseason. The players they did sign, Shawn Armstrong, Colin Holderman and Connor Brogdon, have ERAs of 4.66, 6.00 and 6.75, respectively, and none have been worth positive bWAR. So, let’s go with DeLauter, who had a cup of coffee during last year’s AL Wild Card Series and made his season debut this year. He’s cooled down massively since his red-hot start since his last home run on April 3, but he’s not striking out and is making good contact. There are still 138 games left in the season, and rookies often go through the ebbs and flows of baseball. The red ink on DeLauter is legit, so things will even out at some point. — Flores

Record: 15-8
Last Power Ranking: 24

Best newcomer: Brock Burke

After a late wild-card push, the Reds opted to largely run it back for the 2026 season, making some bullpen additions on the periphery, re-signing closer Emilio Pagán and bringing back fan-favorite Eugenio Suarez on a one-year deal, so there isn’t too much to pick from. That said, Burke has been a pleasant bullpen surprise. The left-hander has allowed just one earned run over his first 10 appearances (9 1/3 innings). Batters are whiffing at 40 percent of his pitches, and his strikeout percentage (29.4 percent) has never been higher. When batters do make contact, they are barreling the ball, so there’s bound to be some regression. For now, Burke has been a welcome addition to Cincinnati’s pen. — Flores

Record: 12-10
Last Power Ranking: 16

Best newcomer: Steven Matz

The Rays’ decision to sign Matz — who was coming off a season spent largely in relief and some mediocre results the last time he was a starter — as a veteran for the rotation felt curious at the time. But the 35-year-old left-hander has justified it so far, with three wins and a sub-4.00 ERA through four starts. He’s more or less swapped out his curveball for a slider and upped his changeup usage against righties, which has allowed him to be the rare rotation convert whose strikeout rate has increased as a starter. — Britton

Record: 11-13
Last Power Ranking: 26

Best newcomer: Adam Frazier?

The Angels have stayed afloat early despite mediocre production from their new guys. The organization gambled on injury-prone starter Grayson Rodriguez — acquired from Baltimore for Taylor Ward — only to see him sidelined almost immediately. Other newcomers on the Angels’ injured list include potential closer Kirby Yates and free-agent flier Alek Manoah. Jordan Romano and Drew Pomeranz have stepped into leverage roles in the Angels’ bullpen, which was going all right until Romano blew two games against the Yankees last week. Meanwhile, Ward’s replacement, Josh Lowe, is off to a miserable start. The hot-starting newcomers have been Frazier and … Brent Suter? It’s not what the Angels were hoping for when they drew up a blueprint for this season. — Nesbitt

Record: 11-12
Last Power Ranking: 15

Best newcomer: Taylor Ward

Well, phew, it would have been odd to recognize a player like Ward here, acquired so much for his right-handed power, if he were still homerless three weeks into the season. Instead, he hit his first long ball on Sunday, part of a really strong start to his first year with the O’s. Ward hasn’t lacked for extra-base pop: His 11 doubles lead baseball. He’s fit right in with Gunnar Henderson at the top of a Baltimore order still waiting for Pete Alonso to get hot. — Britton

Record: 11-11
Last Power Ranking: 18

Best newcomer: Josh Bell

After a massive deadline sell-off, the Twins are .500, and Bell is the leader in many of their offensive categories, including average, slugging, OPS, hits, RBIs, doubles, and is tied for the lead in home runs with three and runs scored with 17. Bell’s 135 wRC+ is his highest since 2019, his lone All-Star season with the Pittsburgh Pirates. Signed to a one-year, $7 million deal, Bell will undoubtedly be one of the biggest players available at the trade deadline as a cost-effective, switch-hitting first baseman and DH. For now, he’s helping lead a surprising Twins team. — Flores

Record: 11-12
Last Power Ranking: 19

Best newcomer: Owen Caissie

The prize return in the Edward Cabrera trade, Caissie is really good when he makes contact. His barrel percentage and average exit velo are in the 90th percentile in the sport — impressive numbers for a 23-year-old with a dozen games of big-league experience before this season. The key is, you know, making contact. Caissie’s 42 percent strikeout rate is the worst in baseball, and the issue is less about chase than it is about swinging through pitches in the zone. — Britton

Record: 8-14
Last Power Ranking: 6

Best newcomer: Andrew Painter

It hasn’t been the newcomers in Painter and Justin Crawford that have hurt the Phillies early this season. While Crawford’s defense in center field has drawn some negative marks, he has held his own offensively in the bottom third of Philadelphia’s order. Painter hasn’t gone deep into games, but he’s kept the Phillies in each start, and you’ll take a five-to-one strikeout-to-walk ratio from anyone, let alone from a 23-year-old rookie’s first month in the majors. Even with Zack Wheeler about to return, Painter’s rotation spot is secure. — Britton

Record: 9-13
Last Power Ranking: 13

Best newcomer: Willson Contreras

Contreras has been more than just the right-handed bat the Red Sox needed to balance their lineup. He’s provided veteran ballast for a young lineup enduring some tough slumps early this season. Contreras’ contact numbers are once again among the game’s best, he’s been excellent at first base defensively, and he’s cut down on some chase to up his walk rate early. He’s been the best of Boston’s offseason pickups by far. — Britton

Record: 9-13
Last Power Ranking: 14

Best newcomer: Dylan Cease

Not a lot has gone right for the Jays to start the season, including with Kazuma Okamoto at third base, but Cease has been everything they could have hoped for in the rotation. The right-hander’s ERA and FIP are both below 2.00 through four starts, and he’s punching out 36 percent of opposing hitters, good for third in the league. He’s diversified his mix by relying a little less on his four-seamer and slider, and he’s getting his actual ERA to align with his peripherals better than he did in San Diego last season. — Britton

Record: 13-9 
Last Power Ranking: 28

Best newcomer: Ramón Urías

The Cardinals made more major-league subtractions than additions this offseason, and the additions they did make (Dustin May, Ryne Stanek, Yohel Pozo, Justin Bruihl) have not been very good. Unlike that quartet, Urias has at least been serviceable. He has a 113 wRC+ over 16 games. Though his defense has been bad by fWAR standards, he’s been asked to wear several hats. He has defensive innings at first, third and shortstop, and is also listed on the Cardinals’ depth chart for second base, too. — Flores

Record: 12-11
Last Power Ranking: 23

Best newcomer: Aaron Civale

The Civale signing looked brilliant through three starts as he cruised through the Braves, Yankees and Mets on the road. Then came a soft matchup against the White Sox … but at home this time. Civale is quickly learning that pitching in West Sacramento can create some strange home/road splits. He was tagged for 11 hits and five runs by the White Sox.

Among the A’s other newcomers, Andy Ibáñez is not yet doing his thing — hitting lefties — but Jeff McNeil is doing his thing — leading off and getting on base at a steady clip. In the bullpen, Joel Kuhnel and Mark Leiter Jr. are both in the mix for saves, and Scott Barlow has been solid outside of one poor outing. — Nesbitt

Record: 10-13
Last Power Ranking: 25

Best newcomer: Foster Griffin

Back in the states after three years in Japan, Griffin has been better at providing the kind of basic competence the Nats need in their rotation than either Miles Mikolas or Zack Littell to this point. He’s throwing seven different pitches at least eight percent of the time, and while he doesn’t have the peripherals to support an ERA down near three, even with some regression, he can be an average big-league starter. That’s something Washington needs as much as anyone else. — Britton

Record: 7-15
Last Power Ranking: 10

Best newcomer: Freddy Peralta

For a team that added Peralta, Bo Bichette, Jorge Polanco, Luis Robert Jr., Devin Williams and Marcus Semien, this figured to be a competitive category. It is, but for the wrong reasons. Bichette and Semien haven’t hit, Polanco’s on the IL, Williams blew his first save chance in two weeks on Sunday, and Robert’s hot start was hurt by a 4-for-31 stretch. So Peralta wins by default — “the two sweetest words in the English language,” as famed astronaut Homer Simpson would tell you. The ERA over four is misleading; six of the last eight runs he’s allowed came after he left the game. And the Mets’ three losses in his starts are by scores of 1-0, 2-1 and 4-2. — Britton

Record: 9-15
Last Power Ranking: 20

Best newcomer: Kai-Wei Teng

Things are trending toward dire in Houston as injuries decimate the rotation. Rookie Tatsuya Imai is among those injured, nursing a tired arm and struggling to adjust stateside. Fellow newcomers Mike Burrows, Peter Lambert and Ryan Weiss are all lugging around ERAs north of 6. The shorthanded rotation is forcing the bullpen to work overtime — a unit already missing Josh Hader and free-agent add Nate Pearson. The Astros are now relying heavily upon Enyel De Los Santos, who was signed last August, to close games, given Bryan Abreu’s early-season issues. One bright spot: Teng, the righty acquired from the Giants this offseason, has been excellent in a multi-inning relief role, posting a 1.98 ERA across 13 2/3 innings. His sweeper is ruthless. — Nesbitt

Record: 7-16
Last Power Ranking: 21

Best newcomer: Eli Morgan

After a particularly rough second half with the Cubs after a deadline deal from the Guardians (12.27 ERA in seven games), Morgan signed a minor-league deal with the Royals over the offseason. He didn’t make the Opening Day roster, but got the call ahead of an early April doubleheader where he pitched three scoreless innings against the Royals before being optioned. A bullpen reshuffle gave him another shot, and so far, so good. Granted, it’s only been five games, but over 8 innings, he has a 1.13 ERA, showing he can fill in as a long man or middle relief. If he can keep it up over the remainder of the season, Morgan is the type of low-key signing that often means the difference for clubs between the postseason and a vacation in Cancun. — Flores

Record: 9-13
Last Power Ranking: 27

Best newcomer: Luis Arraez

Arraez remains one of the most predictable hitters in the sport, even if he’s not vying for batting titles. In San Francisco, Arraez is batting .305 and running the lowest strikeout rate in the sport. What has changed about Arraez’s production (in this tiny sample) is his glove. His defense at second base has already been worth 4 Outs Above Average. For context, Arraez has never finished a season with a positive OAA at the position, entering this season with a career -37 OOA at second base. I don’t understand it. But I stand in awe of it.

Elsewhere, backup catcher Daniel Susac is screamin’ hot and reliever Caleb Killian has been sharp, but the rotation remains a concern. It seems Adrian Houser and Tyler Mahle were not the answers. — Nesbitt

Record: 9-14
Last Power Ranking: 29

Best newcomer: Troy Johnston

Waived by the Marlins last fall, Johnston has taken a liking to the confines of Coors Field, where he terrorized the Dodgers over the weekend. Johnston is slashing .323/.382/.516 (.898 OPS) in 19 games. The Rockies’ other new hitters should take pointers. Here’s how they stack up by OPS+, where 100 is average: Edouard Julien: 92, TJ Rumfield: 85, Willi Castro: 64, Brett Sullivan: 64, Jake McCarthy: 62.

As for the new arms, starter Tomoyuki Sugano has had three good starts and an ugly one (and not a single wild pitch yet for the guy who led the league in ’em last year); reliever Brennan Bernardino has allowed just one earned run; and veteran starters Michael Lorenzen and José Quintana both have ERAs over 5.5. — Nesbitt

Record: 8-14
Last Power Ranking: 30

Best newcomer: Munetaka Murakami

Few players epitomize three true outcomes quite like Murakami. He has eight home runs to his name, including homers in each of the past three games. That’s enough for third in the league. He’s in the top 10 for strikeouts with 31. He’s also third in walks. He’s barreling the ball more than Shohei Ohtani, with exit velocity rates higher than Yordan Alvarez, the league leader in homers. He’s also striking out nearly as much as Kyle Manzardo, a player with negative fWAR, but walking more than some of baseball’s best eyes. It’s beautiful, and after years of disappointment, White Sox fans can call Murakami their own. — Flores
